title: Technology & Ethics

objectives: Use ethical reasoning and trade-offs to analyze and communicate ideas related to technology & ethics with appropriate C1 complexity.

stages.title: Understand meaning and form
stages.instructions: Read the concept, pattern, examples, contrast, common issue, and recap.

blocks.text: The communicative aim of this lesson is to use ethical reasoning and trade-offs to analyze and communicate ideas related to technology & ethics with appropriate C1 complexity. The central language focus is ethical reasoning and trade-offs. In the context of society, ideas & complex topics, form and meaning work together: first identify the relationship between the ideas, then choose wording that makes that relationship clear to another person. At C1, precision includes stance, register, and information structure. Make the relationship between claims explicit, qualify what cannot be fully supported, and adapt the wording to the audience without losing nuance.

blocks.explanation: This model establishes the main communicative move.

blocks.english: A clear explanation addresses ethical implication directly.
blocks.explanation: This model develops or qualifies the message.

blocks.text: Start with the model “The discussion highlighted uneven impact.” It establishes a useful direction for the exchange. The second model, “A clear explanation addresses ethical implication directly.” adds another layer: a reason, implication, contrast, or response. Notice how each complete chunk does a communicative job. Practice replacing one detail while preserving the original grammar, stance, and register. Then connect the revised sentence to a relevant consequence or example instead of changing topic abruptly.

A useful pattern for this lesson is: ethical reasoning and trade-offs. Use it when the situation genuinely calls for that meaning. Contrast matters: a direct factual statement presents information, while a qualified or hypothetical form changes the speaker's commitment to it. The choice should be driven by evidence, time reference, relationship, and purpose. In listening, pay attention not only to individual words but also to linkers, stress, and the speaker's degree of certainty.

blocks.title: Contrast
blocks.text: Compare a direct statement with language shaped by ethical reasoning and trade-offs; the intended meaning determines the form.

A common issue is to select an advanced-looking form without maintaining its meaning across the sentence. That can create a mismatch in time, stance, or register. Check three things: what happened or is being proposed, how certain the speaker is, and what response is expected. For technology & ethics, clarity comes from a coherent message rather than maximum complexity. The later stages recycle the same vocabulary and expressions so that recognition becomes controlled production and then flexible interaction.

blocks.title: Common issue
blocks.text: Do not add complexity that changes the time reference, degree of certainty, or relationship with the listener.

stages.title: Listen for meaning and stance
stages.instructions: Listen first, then reveal the text and notice connections, register, and emphasis.

segments.text: To begin with, The discussion highlighted uneven impact. A clear explanation addresses ethical implication directly.
In this situation, A clear explanation addresses ethical implication directly. The speaker emphasized informed consent.
From another perspective, The speaker emphasized informed consent. Our response should account for unintended consequence.
More specifically, Our response should account for unintended consequence. This example illustrates equal access clearly.
Even so, This example illustrates equal access clearly. We should consider structural barrier carefully.
As a result, We should consider structural barrier carefully. The discussion highlighted social mobility.
On reflection, The discussion highlighted social mobility. A clear explanation addresses changing workforce directly.
